summary:
São Paulo state stands under Brazil's uniform national framework, which applies identically in all 27 states: same-sex marriage has been legal since May 2013 under National Council of Justice Resolution 175/2013, binding on every civil registry after a 14-1 vote; name and gender-marker changes require no surgery; and spousal-visa equality and joint adoption operate on the same footing as for any other visitor or resident.

On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court ruled in ADO 26 that discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is a crime equivalent to racism under Lei 7.716/1989, punishable by imprisonment and fines. Transphobia is consequently prosecuted on the same footing as racism, and a visitor who faces discriminatory conduct in São Paulo can invoke that provision directly.

No specific federal anti-discrimination statute exists. The 2019 ruling supplies the prohibition, and repeal efforts have been tabled in the National Congress, so the durability of the statutory route is contested even as the constitutional and criminal provisions remain in force. The Superior Court of Justice held in 2023 that nonbinary people may amend their civil records, which bears on how a document carrying a nonbinary marker is read at entry and in services.

São Paulo courts have applied the anti-discrimination provisions to commercial conduct. The 27th Private Chamber of the São Paulo Court of Justice upheld a moral-damage award against a nightclub that refused entry to a trans woman wearing women's clothing, affirming the compensation ordered at first instance in Barra Bonita. Refusal of service on this ground is therefore actionable in this state.

The protective text of the law does not describe what people routinely encounter. Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records that LGBTIQ people still face significant violence and discrimination despite the constitutional and criminal provisions. A May 2024 investigation documented 'boa noite, Cinderela' drink-spiking robberies in which LGBTQIA+ people are targeted in São Paulo nightlife, in a city preparing for a Pride event that draws thousands of tourists. Nightlife carries a documented, targeted risk here that is not captured by the criminal provisions.

The unit led the national ranking in 2024 with 16 killings of travestis and trans people, then fell to 4 recorded killings in 2025, out of the top group. The country's dominant geographic pattern applies: at least 68% of the 2024 killings, 83 of 122, occurred outside state capitals in interior cities, so a traveller's exposure sits more in the interior than in the capital.

Detention carries a specific regime. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, governs where LGBTI people who are arrested or imprisoned are housed. LGBTI status is recognised by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing. On arrest the place of deprivation of liberty is fixed by a judge in a reasoned decision after the person has been consulted: the judge must set out the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units and ask trans, travesti and intersex people whether they prefer custody in a female, male or specific unit, and within it the general population or a specific wing or cell. The declared preference is recorded, a later change of placement is possible, and transfers are prioritised where there is violence or a serious threat. LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.

Practice does not reliably follow that framework. A peer-reviewed census carried out between April and June 2021 in Rio de Janeiro state prisons interviewed 138 self-declared travesti and trans-woman inmates inside eleven units treated as masculine in the metropolitan region, and documents that travestis and trans women are housed in units operated as masculine, with some held in so-called neutral or security units. The study treats placement in male units as a double punishment compounded by recurring violations of basic rights, which is the pattern a trans detainee in this country should expect to encounter rather than the text of Resolution 348.

Protection machinery has widened. An analysis of case law from 2022 records lower courts pressing the Superior Court of Justice toward unanimously extending the remedies of the Maria da Penha Law and the Feminicide Law to trans women, bringing trans people within the country's violence-prevention statutes.

Practical friction varies by settlement size. Larger cities such as São Paulo carry legal infrastructure, including counsel experienced in gender-marker and discrimination matters, while smaller cities and rural areas carry more social friction and thinner support.
tangentialFactors:
Intersex people in Brazil have no specific statutory protections, a gap that sits alongside the otherwise broad framework and affects how an intersex visitor's documents and treatment in care settings are governed.

The 2024 killings figure of 16 placed São Paulo at the head of the national ranking, and the fall to 4 in 2025 tracks a national decline rather than a state-specific intervention; the interior-versus-capital split of 83 of 122 killings outside capitals in 2024 is a country-wide pattern that shapes where risk concentrates for any traveller.

The census evidence on prison placement comes from Rio de Janeiro state rather than São Paulo, so it establishes how the national detention rules have been applied in practice in a comparable large state, not a finding about São Paulo's own prison units.

LGB people serve openly in the Brazilian military and have had adoption rights since 2015, facts that sit on the LGB side of the regime rather than bearing directly on a trans visitor's exposure.

Nonbinary residents have been able to amend civil records since the Superior Court of Justice's 2023 ruling, extending marker recognition beyond the binary options.

In the October 2024 municipal elections close to 1,000 transgender candidates stood across every state of the country and received death threats and intimidation, while the number of trans officeholders tripled compared with the previous cycle.

Lower courts have been pressing the Superior Court of Justice toward unanimously extending the Maria da Penha Law and the Feminicide Law to trans women, which would place trans people squarely within the domestic-violence and feminicide protection machinery.

Residents detained in the state are covered by Resolution 348 and Resolution 366, which require a reasoned judicial placement decision, record the person's own stated preference, permit later changes of placement, and forbid using LGBTI-specific spaces as disciplinary isolation or compulsory transfer as punishment.
